Reproducing a published analysis: prepregnancy BMI in Ontario

Source: vignettes/published-analysis.Rmd
published-analysis.Rmd

Khademioore and colleagues (2026, Canadian Journal of Public Health) studied the prepregnancy body mass index (BMI) of 1.17 million singleton births in Ontario from fiscal year 2012-2013 to 2021-2022. Among other analyses, they fitted a joinpoint regression model to the yearly mean BMI, selecting the number of joinpoints by BIC, and concluded that BMI was stable until 2016 and rose afterwards. Their Table 4 reports:

Segment Period Slope (95% CI) p
1 2012-2016 0.016 (-0.035, 0.067) 0.49
2 2016-2021 0.125 (0.088, 0.162) < 0.001

with a joinpoint at 2016 (95% CI 2014-2019), a slope change of 0.109 per year (p = 0.010), and BIC values of 3.73, 2.93 and 3.33 for the models with 0, 1 and 2 joinpoints.

The article is open access (CC BY 4.0) and its appendix tabulates the yearly data, which ship with the package as ontario_bmi. This vignette reproduces the published analysis in R, draws the trend of Figure 3 with error bars and slope labels, and extends the analysis to the BMI categories. Figure 4 of the article, mean BMI by age group, ethnicity and parity, cannot be reproduced because those yearly series are not published.

The data 

library(joinpoint)
library(ggplot2)
mb <- unique(ontario_bmi[c("year", "births", "mean_bmi", "sd_bmi")])
mb$se <- mb$sd_bmi / sqrt(mb$births)
mb
#>    year births mean_bmi sd_bmi         se
#> 1  2012 107457     25.3    6.2 0.01891361
#> 7  2013 113350     25.3    6.1 0.01811837
#> 13 2014 115375     25.3    6.1 0.01795866
#> 19 2015 118943     25.3    6.0 0.01739730
#> 25 2016 123328     25.3    6.0 0.01708521
#> 31 2017 121714     25.6    6.2 0.01777139
#> 37 2018 120177     25.6    6.2 0.01788467
#> 43 2019 119566     25.7    6.2 0.01793031
#> 49 2020 115034     25.8    6.2 0.01828010
#> 55 2021 116053     26.0    6.3 0.01849321

The standard error of each yearly mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of births. Supplying it makes the fit weighted by the inverse squared standard errors.

The published model

The authors modeled mean BMI on its original scale, so the segments are summarized by slopes in kg/m^2 per year rather than percent changes (log = FALSE), and they selected the number of joinpoints by BIC with at most two joinpoints. The article does not name its interval method; the published intervals are symmetric around the estimates, which points to parametric intervals.

fit <- joinpoint(mb, year, mean_bmi, se = se, log = FALSE, kmax = 2,
                 method = "bic", ci_method = "parametric")
fit
#> Joinpoint regression (linear model, se variance)
#> Model selection: BIC; confidence intervals: parametric
#> 
#> Cohort: All
#>   Joinpoints: 1 (2016)
#>   2012-2016  Slope = 0.016   [-0.040, 0.073]
#>   2016-2021  Slope = 0.125*  [0.085, 0.165]
#>   AAC Full Range (2012-2021) = 0.077*  [0.051, 0.102]
#> 
#> * Significantly different from zero at alpha = 0.05.
#> Intervals are conditional on the selected number of joinpoints.

The selection statistics, the slope change at the joinpoint and the joinpoint itself:

model_selection(fit)$criteria[, c("joinpoints", "sse", "bic", "selected")]
#>   joinpoints       sse      bic selected
#> 1          0 263.69203 3.732714    FALSE
#> 2          1  74.52968 2.929646     TRUE
#> 3          2  70.32048 3.332029    FALSE
est <- model_estimates(fit)
est[est$parameter == "Slope 2 - Slope 1", c("estimate", "se", "p_value")]
#>    estimate         se     p_value
#> 5 0.1087983 0.02688981 0.009863408
joinpoints(fit)
#>   model final  ci_method joinpoint estimate lower upper
#> 1     1  TRUE parametric         1     2016  2014  2017

The package offers two parametric intervals for the joinpoint location. The default contains the candidate years whose best fit with the joinpoint there has a residual sum of squares within Q (1 + k F / (n - p)) of the minimum Q (Lerman 1980), with F the 95% quantile of the F distribution on k and n - p degrees of freedom. The conservative variant, Q (1 + k / (n - p)) F, multiplies the whole bracket by F and gives a wider interval:

fit_lit <- joinpoint(mb, year, mean_bmi, se = se, log = FALSE, kmax = 2,
                     method = "bic", ci_method = "parametric",
                     control = jp_control(tau_interval = "literal"))
joinpoints(fit_lit)[, c("estimate", "lower", "upper")]
#>   estimate lower upper
#> 1     2016  2014  2019

Quantity by quantity, with the package values computed from the fits above:

Quantity Published Package
BIC, 0 to 2 joinpoints 3.73, 2.93, 3.33 3.73, 2.93, 3.33
Joinpoint 2016 2016
Slopes 0.016, 0.125 0.016, 0.125
Segment p values 0.49, < 0.001 0.49, < 0.001
Slope change (p) 0.109 (0.010) 0.109 (0.010)
Slope 95% CIs (-0.035, 0.067), (0.088, 0.162) (-0.040, 0.073), (0.085, 0.165)
Joinpoint 95% CI 2014-2019 2014-2017; variant 2014-2019

A figure with error bars and slope labels

The yearly means and the fitted segments of Figure 3, with the 95% confidence interval of each yearly mean as an error bar and the slope of each segment and its interval written next to the segment. The figures of this article are interactive (see jp_interactive()): hovering a segment shows its period, slope, confidence interval and p value and highlights it, hovering a year shows its mean with its confidence interval and the fitted value, and the toolbar zooms and saves the figure as an image.

g <- autoplot(fit, error_bars = TRUE, labels = "ci", interactive = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Fiscal year (start)", y = expression("Mean BMI (kg/m"^2 * ")"))
jp_interactive(g, width = 7, height = 4.2)

jp_table() gives the manuscript table, including the average annual change (AAC) over the full period, the linear model counterpart of the AAPC:

knitr::kable(jp_table(fit, digits = 3))
Trend Period Slope / AAC (95% CI) p
Segment 1 2012-2016 0.016 (-0.040, 0.073) 0.491
Segment 2 2016-2021 0.125* (0.085, 0.165) < 0.001
AAC 2012-2021 0.077* (0.051, 0.102) < 0.001

Extending the analysis: BMI categories

A mean can hide shifts in the tails. The appendix also gives the number of births in each World Health Organization category, so the prevalence of each category can be analyzed with its binomial standard error. With type = "percent", count and population, joinpoint() computes the percentages and their standard errors. A log-linear model summarizes each period by the relative change in prevalence, the natural scale for prevalences that differ by an order of magnitude.

fit_cat <- joinpoint(ontario_bmi, year, count = count, population = births,
                     by = "category", type = "percent", kmax = 2,
                     method = "bic", ci_method = "parametric")

On a logarithmic axis the parallel shape of the obesity classes and the divergence of underweight and normal weight stand out:

g <- autoplot(fit_cat, layout = "overlay", labels = "none", error_bars = TRUE,
              log_y = TRUE, interactive = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Fiscal year (start)", y = "Prevalence (%)")
jp_interactive(g, width = 7, height = 5)

Panels colored by trend direction show where each category turned:

g <- autoplot(fit_cat, color_by = "trend", error_bars = TRUE, aapc = TRUE,
              interactive = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Fiscal year (start)", y = "Prevalence (%)")
jp_interactive(g, width = 8, height = 6)

The overweight and underweight series turn in 2016, the year the mean turned, while obesity class I was already rising from 2014. Obesity class II rose steadily over the whole decade. The full set of trends:

knitr::kable(jp_table(fit_cat, digits = 2))

Khademioore S, Darling EK, D’Souza R, Muraca GM, Guo Y, Anderson LN (2026). Prepregnancy body mass index in Ontario from 2012 to 2022: a population-based descriptive study. Canadian Journal of Public Health. doi:10.17269/s41997-026-01214-w
